title: Analysis of Protein Inhibitors of Trypsin in Quinoa, Amaranth and Lupine Seeds. Selection and Deep Structure-Function Characterization of the Amaranthus caudatus Species
content: Protein protease inhibitors are biomolecules with growing biological, biotechnological and biomedical relevance, including those derived from plants. In this work, we compared by Intensity-Fading.Mass Spectrometry (IF-MS) and other approaches the occurrence of strong protein protease inhibitors against trypsin-type enzymes in seeds from plants of quinoa, amaranth and lupine traditionally used in South America. We differentially found that although amaranth seeds have the smaller quantity of aqueous soluble and thermostable protein material, they show the highest level of trypsin inhibitory capability among them. Such property was directly assigned by HPLC, MS/MS and activity measurements of the seed extracts to a single protein form of 7889.1 Da. It appeared identical in two studied amaranth variants, Amaranthus caudatus and A. hybridus, showing in both a Ki of 1.24nM for the canonical bovine trypsin. The high homogeneity and easy scalability found for this protein form, together with the outstanding nutritional quality of its seeds, prompted us to further structurally and functionally analyse it. This form succesfully crystallised with the above enzyme. The 3D structure of the complex, solved at 2.8 Å resolution by X-ray crystallography, displayed the inhibitor and enzyme trapped in a substrate-like transition state mode, unveiling the structure-function basis of the inhibitory and specific interactions. It verified that this trypsin inhibitor can be classified within the potato-I structural family, with its single disulfide constraining the binding loop as a key feature. Cell culture studies showed that the inhibitor addition is not affecting the cell growth capability of distinct plant microbial pathogen models, as diverse bacteria and fungi, or parasite models such as Mycoplasma genitalium and Plasmodium falciparum. Such overall behaviour seems to disfavour a role of the inhibitor as antimicrobial, and in potentially related agricultural/biotech/biomed uses, and suggests the convenience to redirect its functional and applicative research towards insect deterrence.
